system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:c59838ca42ab",
  "problem": "Whether the evaluation proxy is worth building given that anyone with sampling access could simply run the counterfactual.",
  "did": "They chose to build a proxy evaluation with clear ground truth whose questions mirror real use cases, accepting that performance is not directly useful.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating hypothesis generation rather than hypothesis discrimination"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Interpretability tools are most needed where no ground truth exists, so a proxy with checkable answers is the only way to measure reliability; failing on it is a bad sign for harder cases."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:ea22a504e027",
  "problem": "How to interpret why a rank-1 adapter and a single steering vector achieve non-trivial verbalization.",
  "did": "They concluded that IAs elicit a latent self-knowledge capability rather than teaching a new capability.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "teaching models a fundamentally new capability"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Even a rank-1 LoRA adapter and a single steering vector perform reasonably, indicating the behavioral information is already accessible and needs only light elicitation."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:98a62568a87b",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that the agents' failures bound the real-world risk of the models.",
  "did": "They explicitly stated the agents are not a robust upper bound on model capability and limited the conclusion to casual users.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The agents they built do not capture the full abilities of the model."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:1fb1577afe9f",
  "problem": "How to obtain large, diverse, correct supervised data of experiments on a subject model.",
  "did": "Scrape science-of-ML arXiv papers for experiment descriptions, have an AI write Python for them, and collect ground truth by executing the code.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Because outputs come from running the code, results stay grounded even if the LM's translation is not faithful to the paper."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:61558b42c52a",
  "problem": "Whether to include unflattering claims about companies that were not strongly supported or central.",
  "did": "They refrained from making unflattering claims that were neither solidly defensible nor relevant to the core assessment, and avoided inviting comparisons between companies.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "inviting salient comparisons between companies on capabilities or safety"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The claims were neither solidly defensible nor particularly relevant to the core assessment."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:7e1d2c539d4e",
  "problem": "Which activation tokens to supply as AO input for secret-keeping evaluations, given that token selection affects performance.",
  "did": "They used the full sequence of activations as the default for all secret-keeping evaluations while reporting that single-token or short selections can do better on some tasks.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "single-token inputs on Taboo",
   "shorter selected sequences for Gender"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Simplicity and consistency, and in real auditing without ground-truth labels it is hard to sweep token selection as a hyperparameter."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:6c9217be2719",
  "problem": "How much to trust the headline doubling-time estimate for task horizon, given noise and methodological choices.",
  "did": "METR ran a sensitivity analysis over data noise and methodological choices, reported a range of doubling times rather than a point estimate, and applied a mental correction for eval-friendly tasks being easier than real tasks.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "reporting a single six-month doubling time"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Tasks that make good automatically scorable evals may be systematically easier for models, so absolute horizons may overstate real-world ability, though the exponential trend is solid."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:117aed529f22",
  "problem": "How to establish that a model believes a statement is false so that its output can be labeled a lie rather than a mistake.",
  "did": "They operationalized beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts without pressure to lie, and used this to label on-policy outputs.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "off-policy false statements",
   "a common-sense notion of lying requiring belief awareness during the lie"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Deceptive intent is hard to verify in LLMs, so a measurable non-deceptionist, assertion-based definition strikes a balance between usefulness and measurability."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:9149fe455ebd",
  "problem": "Why LLM-as-a-Judge performed unexpectedly poorly on HP-C, and whether label noise from incorrect beliefs was responsible.",
  "did": "They manually reviewed misclassifications and re-ran the judge with modified prompts and on belief-correct subsets, finding that the judge's failure to spot incorrect expert-knowledge answers was the main cause rather than incorrect beliefs.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "incorrect beliefs in the labels as the main cause"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "AUROC only rose to 0.76 when restricted to correct beliefs, but rose to 0.82 when the judge scored incorrectness instead of lying."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:2c5b2536a78c",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the cross-model result for everyday safety questions on Qwen3-30B-A3B.",
  "did": "They hedged the claim. They said Negation Neglect transfers less readily to overt harmful advice than to subtler power-seeking and manipulative behaviors.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The negated model shows substantially lower rates on most everyday safety questions."
 }
]
